analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fracking exemption from the Safe Drinking Water Act and requires disclosure of fracturing chemicals.
analysis.headline: The FRAC Act never got a vote in the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee; it sat there from April 2017 until the Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, hydraulic fracturing (fracking) is exempt from the Safe Drinking Water Act's rules for injecting fluids underground. The bill would end that exemption, letting the EPA regulate fracking injections under the drinking-water law. It would also require companies to disclose, before and after each fracking operation, what chemicals they inject, post that list publicly, and hand over trade-secret chemical identities to doctors and first responders during a medical emergency.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations and rely on nearby groundwater, along with medical workers who need to know what chemicals a patient may have been exposed to. In states that take over enforcement, state environmental agencies would gain a clear authority to regulate fracking directly.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near fracking sites and first responders

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the 2005-style exemption that keeps hydraulic fracturing outside the Safe Drinking Water Act, so fracking fluid injections would be regulated as underground injection rather than going unreviewed [S2] [S3].

Companies would have to report, before and after each operation, every chemical and propping agent injected, with chemical identification numbers and quantities, and the state or EPA must verify the information and post it on a single public searchable website [S2] [S3].

In a medical emergency, companies must immediately hand a trade-secret chemical's identity to a doctor, first responder, the state, or the EPA on request, without waiting for paperwork or a confidentiality agreement [S2] [S3].

The bill also lets a state take primary enforcement responsibility for fracking alone, without taking over regulation of every other type of injection well, lowering the barrier for states to police fracking directly [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers who use fracking would bear the cost of tracking and reporting chemical use and the possibility of EPA or state permits for injections. Some companies argue disclosure threatens trade secrets, though the bill preserves trade-secret formulas from public release and limits who can share emergency disclosures.

drawbacks.text: The bill protects proprietary chemical formulas from public disclosure [S2] [S3], but industry groups have long argued that even filing chemical identities with regulators risks exposing competitive information and could slow drilling [S3].

Additional federal permitting and reporting under the Safe Drinking Water Act would add compliance costs to fracking operations, which industry says could raise production costs in a business with thin margins [S2].
The bill does not fund new EPA or state inspectors, so oversight would depend on existing agency capacity [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is knowing what is being pumped into the ground near drinking water and getting fast chemical answers in an emergency; the cost falls on a specific industry in the form of reporting and possible permitting. The trade-secret carve-out and the option for states to take over enforcement soften the industry's burden while keeping the transparency mandate intact.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Bob Casey introduced the bill on April 6, 2017, with ten Democratic cosponsors including Schumer, Durbin, Feinstein, and Whitehouse [S3] [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works that same day, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
The bill died in committee at the end of the 115th Congress without a vote in either chamber [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers keep the fracking exemption and face no federal disclosure mandate; they benefit from the bill's death.

against.name: Senate Republican majority

sides.party_line_note: All 11 supporters were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and it never advanced past referral.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers using hydraulic fracturing
industries.note: The bill would subject fracking injections to Safe Drinking Water Act regulation and require chemical disclosure, adding compliance costs; in exchange, the public gains transparency about what goes into wells near drinking water. The industry's interest in keeping the exemption runs against residents' interest in disclosure.

industries.industry: State environmental agencies in fracking states
industries.note: The bill lets a state take primary enforcement over fracking without regulating all other injection wells, a new authority for state regulators.
